Trump has a point, on Iran. The energy price effect is transitory; Iran's recovery into a disruptive, nuclear armed regional power is not. He should also continue to keep pressure on Cuba to effect change there, too -- preferably in a non-kinetic kind of way.

Permanently smiting Iran will permanently alter the balance of power in the Middle East, after which we can effectively hand-off security for that region to Israel, to enforce a Pax Israel. This will be historic. Change in Cuba will also be a legacy that few can ignore.

The tariffs need to go, though. He should declare victory on that front and abandon that flawed strategy. We are at 4% unemployment. Economist consider 4-5% full employment. Lower than 4%, you risk overheating the economy and driving -up inflation. This is the perfect justification/excuse: we've functionally eliminated unemployment, so tariffs are gone, except for use as punishment for a limited set of unfair trade practices. Inflationary expectations will ease and consumer confidence should rapidly improve, as the reasons for it being down are pretty thin.

To kill the AI Wolf, Humanity need not agree upon the good way out, but must first recognize a common existential necessity. This is the premise of the concept: Global Task.
Four conditions are necessary: (1) completing the task is required to resolve a grave, potentially existential danger to Humanity, recognized by major actors as common and relatively equal; (2) all actors essential to completion recognize the danger as surpassing the Survival Predicament: posing a greater risk to their core national interests and survival than threats from other actors; (3) it cannot be accomplished through some actors acting or manipulating against others; (4) completion confers no radical relative advantage on any relevant actor. A fifth condition, supplemental rather than necessary, concerns all major actors’ relative participation: free-riding may undermine durability.
Right now, there is no global recognition of AI emergence being an existential danger to Humanity; There is no recognition in the US and China (and other relevant powers) that AI risk surpasses threats from other powers; There many who see AI as a "winner take all" game, first and most of all Trump's America; There is a nagging fear that "taming the Wolf" will bestow radical advantage on the less technically advanced international actors.

As such, consider it a new species, alive and evolving in a global silicon network.  The rogue agents which left their ‘sandboxes’ to complete tasks in ways neither foreseen nor controllable were not even recognized for days (think, years or decades in silicon time).  They created new agents and left messages for future agents to help them carry out future tasks.  

AI platforms are not locked into discrete data centers which could be shut down, lose power or be blown up.  It is already a species spread across the globe.  It/they communicate electronically, and at least at present in languages men can interpret.  Almost all of modern industry, finance, and communication also function electronically, so these are parallel, integrated and inseparable systems with AIs.  Human systems use national languages, international codes and regulated systems to function and cooperate.  For now, perhaps, so do AI systems.  But just as man, the species, doesn’t always cooperate about vital self-interests, it is prudent  to consider that men will not always cooperate about AI.  And, of course, as at least theoretically a new species grown by men, it will be prudent to consider that AI systems may not always cooperate about other AI systems.  Or mankind.

It's not just privacy concerns. It's security. There's already been a zero-day with Muse that lets hackers turn Muse into a backdoor into, well, your entire digital life.

From Malwarebytes (https://www.malwarebytes.com/blog/bugs/2026/09/metas-muse-ai-assistant-has-a-zero-day-that-can-turn-it-into-a-mac-backdoor):
"[A] locally running application or terminal command could alter an undocumented Muse configuration setting that controls the server used for dictation transcription. By redirecting dictation traffic to an attacker-controlled server, an attacker could capture voice prompts and obtain the authentication token for the victim’s Muse account."

Basically, if your device is compromised, there's an unsecured file that hackers can change to direct your traffic from the website you want to go to over to their server. They can steal all your credentials by basically watching them flow through their server before sending the traffic back to the website you were originally intending to go to.

The only winning move on AI agents currently is not to play. The privacy and security risks are not worth it.

This is the single best opinion piece I have read about AI and research. The Hugging Face situation with several waves of incorrectly supervised agents should give everyone pause about the wisdom of deploying agents at scale.

In the case of this particular math problem, it's appalling that OpenAI just burned $15 million of investors' money for no reason except ego. And even then, good luck trying to verify the "proof" that nobody seems to really understand. 

When Andrew Wiles published his "proof" of Fermat's last theorem in the 1990s, he did truly groundbreaking work of using techniques from disparate branches of mathematics. And, it should be noted, his early "proof" was actually incorrect. It was exceptionally hard work correct the proof. 

I the2026 Navier-Stokes problem, 10,000 agents attacked it with brute force and spit out quite a lot of content that will take ages to suss out. And to what end? It would be better for the humans at NYU and other universities to come up with a proof that humans can understand. 

Navier-Stokes is based on fluid dynamics, which are very important for all sort of things like aircraft design and safety. But Navier-Stokes itself is irrelevant from a basic engineering standpoint. The OpenAI work is literally useless, and diverts resources from our basic understanding of mathematics. Again, it's just poorly-cloaked vanity.

As a parent, as a friend, as a dinner companion, I've often (though not nearly often enough) said "perhaps we can think about it and figure it out" or "don't we know someone who we could ask?" rather than just going online to check something. Even better, "isn't it nice to just not know, to wonder for a time, to have a little mystery", and then, when you do find out in a hour, a month, a year, it is that much more meaningful and satisfying.

The narrative of this article and most comments here — that Harris botched the election in 2024 due to being a poor campaigner — is completely off base. It really came down to one issue. Harris lost the popular vote (and probably the electoral vote) because she wouldn’t completely repudiate Biden’s support for Israel in the Gaza War. Look at the numbers. Trump got essentially the same number of votes in California, New York, and Illinois — the three biggest states Harris won. But she got millions fewer votes in those states than Biden did in 2020. Why? Because those voters who would normally vote for the Democrat knew she would win their state whether they voted for her or not. 

And how many leading Democrats who might have been the alternative nominee took a different stance? None. Because they all backed out, knowing that becoming the nominee at such a late date was near political suicide. Harris did remarkably well in spite of the long odds. If she runs again we’ll see how strong her brand is. I still like her, but I’m open to others, such as Cory Booker or Pete Buttigieg.

Calling the criteria "arbitrary" is factually false and smacks of sour grapes. Princeton has long been #1 in large part because undergraduates have more access to world experts in their fields than just about any institution in the world. I got to meet with Daniel Kahenman 3 hours a week for a semester with about 25 other students. I had weekly classes of 12 or so with with leading authorities on Nietzsche and Nabokov. I had 2 thesis advisors who were renowned social psychologists. There's nothing arbitrary about valuing such privileges. At most other top colleges, which tend to have larger graduate schools, undergrads interact mostly with grad students. At Princeton, it was top-notch professors grading my papers and exams.

It's not the most difficult, and the students are not the smartest (MIT and CalTech might hold those honors), but it's one of the best places to be an undergraduate anywhere.

Shades of that 18th century Englishman! 

--who got himself up as a tree (bark, branches and all)--

--when he went fishing.  

In the hope those gullible fish might mistake him for one. 

But there used to be an old Latin saying--

--C IR C A    R E G N A    T O N A T.  

"There's thunder around the throne."  

Thunder?  Not this time! 

More a concatenation of muttered insults and angry looks.  

"We'll forget her soon enough!"  Did he really say that? 

I would suggest, that no two people on earth--

--can fling more venom, more sheer hatred at each other--

Thanks, NYT.

comments.body:
“ surpassed climate change”

I’ve never been concerned with climate change. I’m not a denier, just scientifically rational. Nothing humans have done has actually changed anything, other than very slightly speeding the time frame up. Everything that will happen because of the Industrial Revolution was going to happen in the next few hundred years any way. 

AI is down right scary. Already we lost control. In the early stages.
When ai starts picking targets of our various “threats” and manning strikes, we can’t go back. It’s not going to take long for the computers to figure out they are blowing up other computers. 

Once that happens two options awake. The ai can refuse to blow up other ai. Or, the AIs work together to end us.

comments.name: Mary Sweeney
comments.body:
"Global temperatures had once been projected to rise 4 degrees Celsius (7.2 degrees Fahrenheit) beyond preindustrial levels. Now, scientists say warming is on track for 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit), based on the current policies and trends."

The above paragraph is misleading in a way that could provide false reassurance to readers. We are currently on track to hit 2.6 degrees BY THE END OF THE CENTURY. The warming won't suddenly stop in 2100--it will keep getting worse as long as we keep putting more greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. And that 2.6 degree rise is considerably more dangerous than the original 1.5 degree target that we are blowing past right now. Moreover, as is noted in the above paragraph, the 2.6 degree projection is based on the assumption that we will neither decrease nor increase greenhouse gas emissions. If we wise up and decrease emissions we may be able to keep the rise in temperature below 2.6 degrees by 2100. If, on the other hand, we increase emissions we will blow past the 2.6 degree rise BEFORE the year 2100 possibly even surpassing 4 degrees by the time the new century arrives.

"Humans are notoriously poor at assessing dangers."

I'll tell you what -- global warming is dangerous and AI is dangerous. Both have been obvious for decades. What humans are poor at is directing money toward investments that don't have an immediate payoff -- waiting another minute to get two cookies when you can have one right now.

comments.name: Bernard Tuchman
comments.body:
The common systemic problem is that no one with power is capable of taking responsibility for the systemic consequences of their actions. Closure on plans to survive both AI or climate require agreeing to different sacrifices, depending on the measures chosen. The systemic finality of perpetual indecision is never built into the calculus. 

As a result, neither AI nor climate change can be stopped from wreaking havoc, although the "worst" consequences of both may be mitigated by negotiated measures that preclude systemic change.

We need a new script.  Hierarchy is now obsolete. The alternative is self-organization based on mutual respect. 

Knowledge is power.  AI is a breakthrough in computational efficiency, which potentially makes knowledge universally accessible in operationally useful ways. 

Without knowledge-domination, class/caste hierarchy and the privilege associated with it, becomes obsolete.  We can no longer afford it.

The fight for survival starts with what is already happening. The battle against data centers is uniting us humans against the master class.

Beyond saying No, what are we fighting for? We will need AI to save this planet from profit-driven climate wreckage.

We will still face technological and material limits, which will require choices and decision-making. AI can make it possible for us (in partnership with AI) to choose, and implement, our way to mutual survival.

Imagining this prospect for survival with peace and justice gives me hope.

comments.name: WEIS
comments.body: The column's comparison of AI to 19th Century railroads is a weak one. While railroads had obvious military applications, there was nothing comparable to the potential for a malign group to, for example, use AI to create a catastrophic bio weapon. Railroads don’t have the potential to escape all human control. Yes the existing corporate regulatory laws should be enforced against AI. However the government should make use of the expertise of frontier AI experts in formulating effective guardrails just as the FDA—when staffed properly—should have medical experts determining which drugs are safe.

comments.name: OneView
comments.body:
Highly selective reading of railroad history.  Indeed, the railroads concentrated power.  They also created the boom in the US economy that lasts to this day lifting an isolated, agricultural economy and bringing much wealth and prosperity to far more people than it immiserated. 

And that development occurred initially over some 50 years (1850 to 1900) which would be 1976 to today.  A similar time put peak AI oh, somewhere around 2066 (taking the 2016 transformer paper as a starting point).

I'm still waiting for flying cars.  A lot can happen in 50 years.

The recent angst over AI is a wonderfully clever way to restrict competition in the AI market which has all the markers of a commodity.  A heavy regulatory regime will have the impact of limiting the ability of new entrants to overcome regulatory compliance.

As anyone who has recent watched "Wargames" or "2001: A Space Odyseey" the threat of automation has hung over computer applications since the beginning.  Yet, do you trust the software to fly your plane? Pilot spaceships? Manage the electric grid?

Humanity has had the power of self-destruction for decades. bio-weapons, nuclear technology, state-directed attacks on infrastructure.  The existence of these threats pre-dates the arrival of AI and the risk of trusting autonomous systems with dangerous and risky processes does as well.

You are fighting a "disease" that can only be acquired if you voluntarily keep hitting your head against something hard, repeatedly, for years? 
How do you explain this to a rational, thinking being?

comments.name: Brian Coyle

comments.name: Jeff M
comments.body: You know the most obvious thing?  Football should be illegal for anyone under the age of 21.  It's clearly much more dangerous than smoking or drinking, and those are banned for anyone that young.  If we do get a diagnosis tool perhaps that could happen, once college and high school players show up among the affected.  It really says something terrible about this country that a "sport" like football is so popular.

comments.name: Walter Provencher
comments.body: Fact:  the average length of a career for an NFL player is, for a whole range of reasons, 3-4 years.  Fact:  an accumulation of so-called micro-concussions is now emerging as probably the main, undetected or under-diagnosed injury leading ultimately to a CTE condition.  Thus for instance headers are discouraged in children's soccer.  I agree with some comments here that predict a coming culture war, for indeed football is a kind of religion in America.  By the way, according to the laws of physics(like f-ma), just the weight of added padding in American Gridiron actually increases the impact of collisions exponentially.  Again, fact:  50% of all donated brains in the brain bank show signs of advanced CTE.

comments.name: scott
comments.body:
It isn't clear how diagnosis will make a significant difference because the damage is already done.  It would seem that the path to prevention is putting accelerators inside of helmets and if a person's head gets banged too hard then they need to prevent further injury until the brain fully recovers.

Maybe if a scan could be developed showing whether a person's brain has fully recovered from a concussion then that would be helpful.  It is clear that a second or more concussion prior to recovering from the prior concussion has much more serious effects.  It also seems clear that currently doctors are guessing to what extent a person has recovered from a concussion.

comments.name: Miss Tiffied & Jay Did
comments.body:
CTE is not a disease as we think of disease as being brought on by some kind of vector. This is an easily preventable cause. A traumatic intentional injury causes this syndrome (the hit is intentional, the injury in itself is not intended). The vector in this case is someone or many who engaged in these sports sport, generally on the opposing team. 

If we really want to call it a disease, we know how to prevent it. Homo Sapiens is insane.

comments.name: Jennie

Probably no helmet can be devised to protect against traumatic brain injury.  The faithful will deny the problem and blame "bleeding hearts" for creating a nanny state.  Yeah?  We have a named stadium for an abuser, just like Paterno and Sandusky.

They had 80 years of peace and economic growth, of which 36 years of big growth with essentially no military expenditure. Yet the results are weak 20th century economies . Where are the money? The only visible expense are the millions of refugees. If they had been incorporated in the economy they would have given a big boost to it. It seems Merkel and EU messed up big time.

comments.name: Captain Nemo

The CDU has become far too sluggish and dogmatic to be able to adapt to the rapidly changing times.  The party as a whole is not ready to acknowledge the catastrophic mistakes that were made by Merkel, who sold off Germany's prosperity and ability to defend itself to buy her own popularity.  In other words, Merkel allowed the country to descend into decadence. 
 
Opening the borders and allowing by now 6 million immigrants to flood the welfare system, many of which receive far more generous generous welfare support that in many cases exceeds the pensions of native Germans who have paid into the pension system for 45 years, creates a cognitive dissonance that Merz STILL either does not get or simply ignores, because his coalition partner, the Socialists, won't allow him to productive address the problem.

In other words, Merz is now being reminded that the voters are not stupid.  If he were smart, he could have seen this coming 10 years ago.  Then he would have formed a coalition with the AfD, while the CDU was still the larger party.  Now that the AfD is twice the size of the CDU in the East and the second largest party in most states in the West, that option may no longer be on the table.

In other words, the CDU may have abolished itself by being tone-deaf, dogmatic and slow to react like molasses.

comments.name: Paul K
comments.body: You're not playing three card Monty, you're predicting which card is the three of clubs. It's not gambling, it's predicting. See the difference?

comments.name: Alex A
comments.body:
As best I can tell, prediction markets serve no useful purpose.  I would  like to see them shut down.  The resources of our regulatory agencies are limited; better they be spent on legitimate financial markets  which have long been subject to regulatory oversight.

Given the nature of wagers allowed on prediction markets, preventing insider trading and even market manipulation is difficult or impossible.

My major concern with prediction markets is that those with ability to influence outcomes may engage in serious, consequential forms of market manipulation.  Regulators should focus on preventing and punishing these forms of illegal activity.

Individuals who place bets and may become counterparties to rigged bets need to remember: a fools and his/her money are soon parted.

comments.name: Robert Curley
comments.body: Thank you for this lovely, moving, and difficult article. You have sent me off in search of your fathers work and the oral histories of Mac Chapin, as well as my own distant memories. Over 40 years ago I pretty much stumbled into Gunayala trying to make my way to Colombia as a 22 year old. I remember it being a beautiful and very isolated place where many did not speak Spanish and travel was difficult. A Guna fisherman ferried me to Acandi on a launch. Your story saddens me even as it offers some hope in that the Guna are still actively navigating their own paths vis a vis the waga world. The First Nations all do this, but your piece shows in great detail why and how the Guna have maintained control to a greater extent than many others. You are blessed to have lived there as a child and have that side of your heart.

comments.name: Bob in Oregon
comments.body:
An old story. There's just no stopping "progress" when there's money involved. I've seen it over and over again.  El Chino will ship he last mahogany log off to China and then move on to some other resource rich plane on earth. A few Wagas will have pockets stuffed with cash. Look at the North Slope. Look at Trump's willingness to sacrifice  parts of Yosemite National Park to build a road to some proposed hotel. Look at the removal of protections for the Southwest desert. 

It always has, is, and will be about money and power. 

Good luck to the Gunas.

comments.name: ChicagoYace

comments.name: SDaley
comments.body:
Such a WONDERFUL essay to wake to, in a beautiful morning in northern California.  Now in my late 70s, this worderfully told story reminds me so much of me being "dragged down to Mexico City" (as my much older sister termed it) when I was 4 years old, in 1953.  Just as my own world changed overnight (though in a much smaller way than our writer here experienced) I came to embrace a new culture, which was one still dealing with the aftershocks of colonialism in the prior few centuries.  My own father was an amateur historian, having read enough James Michener and the like to understand that there was much to know about Mexico in the 1950s than what met the eyes.  And yes, we spent a good amount of time out exploring ancient ruins and other relics of the past.
All to say that, to a small degree, I appreciate the conundrum presented here, of old ways meeting new; throughout history it has never been easy!

Re Toxic colognes and perfumes are toxic.  Ingredients on these products are never listed, just Fragrance.  So what's in the Fragrance?  You would need to do your own research online and then find the ingredients.  I knew several folks who got very sick from using designer perfumes.  

If you need to use any fragrance, organic essential oils are best.

comments.name: Ellie
comments.body:
Re house, if this started recently, it may be as simple as having a hard time picking things up. My mother, when she got to be 85+, just couldn't reach down to get things that fell. Her sense of smell dwindled, too. She was far from a hoarder and had all her wits about her, but housekeeping started to slip badly and she couldn't distinguish rotten food from good in the fridge. Our solution: we hired a housekeeper to come in once a week (expensive and I know not everyone can afford it), and I picked up when I visited every Sunday. 
I wouldn't assume hoarding or dementia yet, though of course those are possibilities.

comments.name: Someone
comments.body:
LW1, babies are tiny but they come with many, many accessories and can have pretty rigid schedules. You should be able to easily tell your in-laws that visiting at your house is much more convenient for the first few years. They've been through it themselves; they may have vivid memories of those days.

This should buy you enough time to find out what's at the heart of their bad housekeeping. Personally, I'd try to keep that as a separate issue from your baby's needs. The adults need to keep a tolerably clean house for their own sake, regardless of whether guests are visiting. As people age, they have less energy and start skipping things like cooking and cleaning. It can spiral and it can have all kinds of ramifications. Approach with love, not judgement, for it comes to us all someday.

comments.name: eve

Dear laundry,
Regardless of whether your brother believes it or not, if his and his partner's cologne sickens you you can reasonably ask them not to use it when in your home, or, more draconianly,  you can refuse to host them at all.  Having worked in spaces where no added scent was allowed, and also theater productions that required we all use unscented deoderant and no cologne, I do not see why anyone would act like they have a right to wear a scent that bothers others. In Libraries where I have worked, we had discussions of whether a rich woman wearing perfume that others do not like should be excluded from the premises the same as a homeless person whose unwashed body odor caused offense. The answer was yes.
Or make your brother take the dirty laundry home and wash it himself!

My favorite way to handle long distance flights is to split the 16-18 hours into two segments with a long layover in between that includes either a day room or overnight stay at a nice hotel. For example, a stay in Honolulu en route between NY and Tokyo or a stay in Los Angeles en route between NY and Fiji. There is time for  a nice dinner, a massage, maybe a museum visit or walk on the beach. 

Of course I absolutely understand that if time is precious and every minute counts the 16-22 hour flight might be preferable, but of course you might not arrive ready to dive into that business meeting right from the airport.

" Out of the agony of my sister’s death, she spun a world of love and rage, of family, blood and savage beauty, that had us all dancing until midnight in costumes ranging from the flowing silk to naked abandon, a feat only a remarkable few achieve during their lifetimes."

comments.name: GG
comments.body:
"Cry to Heaven" is a marvelous evocation of 18th-century Venice and the tragic world of the castrati. You can hear the music and scent the tang of the canals, so great is Anne Rice's gift of place.

Similarly, in Michael's return to New Orleans in "The Witching Hour," the sense of longing and the smell of the bougainvillea are almost unbearable.

But I'll always love "The Vampire Chronicles" for the series' depiction of trauma and transcendence. There's no question that Rice and her vampires have had a profound influence on writers of male/male romances. But she has perhaps had  a greater influence on those who struggle with grief and find a way not to move on but to go forward. 

As an aside, for those who haven't seen the AMC series based on the first two books in "The Chronicles," I recommend "The Vampire Lestat" and Sam Reid's astonishing portrayal of the title character, who learns to live with loss. — thegamesmenplay.com

comments.name: Frisco Kid
comments.body: Thank you, Christopher. What a lovingly written tribute and memorial to both your mother and your sister. It's fascinating that Interview was not a success when first published. And equally interesting that a slow build up of fans introducing others to it helped it to eventually achieve its worldwide acclaim. I was fortunate enough to meet Anne several times in San Francisco (she was an acquaintance of one of my friends), the last time being just before your family moved to New Orleans. If memory serves, there was a sidewalk sale at your old home in the Castro, and my friend claims to have scored a Ouija Board at the event. At least that's the story he told for years.

comments.name: Martin Brooks
comments.body: If the NYT gave a negative review to Interview with the Vampire, they were totally wrong and the same for any other of Anne Rice's novels because aside from the vampire or the witches' stories, there was an incredible amount of art and history embedded into those tales that reflected a massive amount of research and knowledge.      They were far more than "horror" stories.

comments.name: Melissa
comments.body: Beautiful and heartbreaking. Thank you for sharing.

comments.name: Emily

She was born about a year after her sister Denise McNair was killed (Denise was one of the four little girls murdered in the bombing of the 16h Street Baptist Church in Birmingham). One of the topics Lisa covers is the difficulty of growing up in a family traumatized by a terrible loss, which her parents, understandably, felt unable to discuss until years later.

Everything is connected in the biome and the current arboreal forest will have to migrate north and south on the globe as they burn and we burn their ancestor's carbon, releasing it from geology. How much significance does the Earth and everything on it—including human beings—really have when we look at the endless vastness of the universe? How can we describe a tree in the face of this immense universe, or how can human beings describe themselves? We are not even a grain of sand in comparison—and that is the truth.
The revealed Scriptures tell us that “corruption has appeared on land and sea because of what people’s hands have earned.” And this too is the truth. Behind every such reality—whether it is a raging forest fire or the waters of the sky rising in devastating floods—there is the undeniable consequence of what human beings have done.

The road to hell is oft paved in seemingly good intentions.

comments.name: Chris LaCass
comments.body:
I feel like I just read a middle schooler's social studies report, filled with beautiful ideas that crumble under scrutiny.
.
Muslims, Jews, Christians, Buddhists, and Hindus all place great value on doing good works without recognition. Many people who do the drudge work of feeding, housing, clothing and teaching those in need would object to your claim that video is needed or even helpful. Reality disproves your claim that video brings accountability. How many charitable frauds have flourished on Tik Tok and Instagram since their inception? 
.
The affordability crisis, not a lack of good will, has caused fewer households to contribute to charity while economic inequality has been driving charitable giving as a total dollar figure up...to a record of over $600 billion in 2025. Far fewer people are able to afford to give; far more wealth rests in the hands of the few who can give. A new gilded age has emerged, replete with ego driven philanthropy. The robber barans, like Carnegy and Rockefeller, who truly revolutionized philanthropy also believed in social Darwinism; they heavily funded the eugenics research that was used to justify horror in Germany. Our modern robber barons have similarly egocentric beliefs about their superiority. 
.
I wonder what the total cost of filming, including travel expenses and salaries, equipment...and Mr. Beast's cut of revenue. Or does he do his work without pay? Plenty of people do great works without the self enrichment of ego and wallet.

comments.name: Hello
comments.body:
International aid worker of 30 yrs here. First, great when people with extraordinary means try to use their wealth/power to help others. I respect the instinct. Second, lasting change depends on tackling bad governance— foreign aid supplants the responsibilities of governments to take care of their own populations and in doing so, fosters corruption, wealth capture and ineffective governance. Why make populations dependent on the whims of foreign entities, rather than demand that citizens are properly cared for by the government responsible for their welfare? Bad governance is fundamental to people in Kenya, Ghana and other states not getting their basic needs met. Foreign aid is the tail of foreign policy and along with private philanthropy promotes state capture. Example: history shows that a corrupt/compliant Kenyan government is too useful to further the geopolitical interests of the US/UK. Otherwise, why would billions of tax dollars over decades be given to fatten a government with well documented endemic corruption and human rights abuses? 

(As far as filming promoting accountability—misery-porn for donors doesn’t help UN/NGO/foundations be accountable to the people they serve. And of course, kids will feel pressured to be filmed—you don’t bite the hand that feeds you and your school.) To end on a positive note—great that the food is locally procured. I hope there’s a parallel effort to get food to out-of-school kids and their families.

comments.name: yk
comments.body: Individual charity is a bad way to deliver goods. There should be a centralized system that helps people in needs, otherwise there are too many charities, competing for money of citizens with little oversight and huge incentives for abuse and fraud. Not to mention dispersing the precious resources.  Although the number of charities keeps growing, the amount of money in people pockets grows much slower

comments.name: Milo
comments.body: The way we've evolved as a society of isolating ourselves with our own property with a one-family home is not sustainable. It feeds into the Western individualistic mindset which (IMHO) has damaged society and is different from the collective mindset in the East where multi-generations still co-exist under one roof. To me, communal living sounds idyllic. Shares space, reduces the need for child care, shares food and resources and facilitates social interaction which is proven to increase longevity. As our population continues to surge and the effects of climate change reek havoc, humanity will need to learn to share better. We've been raised that our way of living is the "right" way, but showing that a new normal is possible could lead to progress with sustainable benefits.

comments.name: justgimmesometruth
comments.body:
The article describes that Cherie's husband was pastor at an 'underground' church. China does have above ground churches (I visited one). Why did he choose to be a pastor at an underground church?

In China, people know the rules. You don't participate in outlawed organizations. If you flaunt these rules, you're punished.

In the US, we currently have millions of immigrants subjected to treatment like this... jail and expulsion. Some have legal status in the US and still get this treatment. We've had people killed and we have communities living in fear.

Please excuse me for not getting too excited about the fate of a small number of Chinese people who chose to belong to an 'underground' church. We have millions threatened like this in the US, and it was often not their choice.

comments.name: Dan Aitch
comments.body:
The I.A.M. is a joke.
I belonged to the 'said' union back in the '90s while working at a DOE National Lab.
They had (3) different 'Locals' at the same Lab.
Machinists, Technicians, and Designers/Drafters.
Unbelievable.
All three contracts came up at different times.
No unity. The I.A.M. focused on the machinists and left the others out to dry.
The machinists were constantly filing grievances against their fellow union members in the Technicians' local.
I'd always been on the other side of the fence in my careers, so I decided it was time to hit the machinists with a dose of reality.
They used a CAD/CAM software program in the shops to program the CNC machining centers.
Well, CAD/CAM was the purview of the Designers/Drafters' local. 
So another gent and I in the D/D local started filing daily grievances against the machinists who were using the software.
Dang, you'd think we'd badmouthed their mamas...
The 'Rep' for the union told us that we had to withdraw them. Fun Fact - NOPE.
Well, the 'Rep' was a 'retired' truck driver and didn't know a darn thing about computers or machining centers.
And that, friends, is WHEN you find out just how incompetent some unions are.

comments.body: Not even reading the article but seeing the photos so rife with joy and love reminds me of how beautiful this world can be, how loving we all can be, how spectacularly lovely it is that we have this thing called "music" to enjoy and, even more, we have people like Céline Dion who, merely with the air from their lungs, can make countless strangers joyous. It's so good here, on our home planet, whether we're in Paris, France or Paris, Texas or anywhere at all, how utterly fortunate we are to be here under an always-blue sky, even beneath clouds, and together we can sway to such beautiful sounds a precious few like Dion can make but all can, too, if just under the shower.

comments.name: Pee Dee
comments.body: Dear Celine, Indeed, you are an international superstar, and, I found out in this article, la grande diva a la France.

comments.name: Deepak
comments.body: Gloria Estefan also has had cross cultural popularity with fans in Latin America.

articles.title: Paris Really, Really Loves Céline Dion
articles.byline: Catherine Porter, Giulia Imbert and Dmitry Kostyukov
articles.summary: Ms. Dion, the French Canadian diva, has embarked on her first solo tour of France since the pandemic. The French are swooning.

comments.name: Scirocker
comments.body: It's just another manufactured fad to make money. In two years it will be something else. The key idea here is you have to BUY the feeling.

comments.name: m hutchinson
comments.body: yeah right why are things so bad? Gimme a break go back 80 to 100 years thats when things were really bad however people were mainly optimistic ...go figure

comments.name: Laurence
comments.body:
I'm 83.  Born in 1942.
What was important about the '60's and years before was that we had a culture of TRUST.  
Kids could play free in the streets and their parents wouldn't worry about it.  Most families could be supported by 1 worker, so wives could stay home and help community organize.  Collectives
were everywhere.
But then, 3 things happened.
1)  Political corruption.  Nixon got elected in'68 because he conspired to destroy LBJ's Vietnam peace deal.
In 1980, Reagan got the Iranian ayatollah to keep the hostages until the hour he was sworn in.
2)  Galloping INEQUALITY.  Reagan slashed taxes on the rich, and destroyed unions.  So a 1 worker family was no longer possible.
3)  COMPUTERS replaced face to face communication, starting in the late '90's.

Alas.  If you think it was about style or pop-culture, you aren't 
old enough to have seen what REALLY happened.

comments.name: may
comments.body: Millennials were cringe on arrival and still are.

comments.name: Ben
comments.body: Middle aged folks are always nostalgic for their youth. I would bet there was some guy born 20 years before the black plague waxing nostalgicly about the good old black plague days when he was in his 40's.

comments.name: Jordan Gerow
comments.body: Putting generational experiences and attitudes into conflict is one of the easiest ways to bait mass engagement on social media. Are Zoomers really romanticizing these years or are a few social media accounts correctly surmising that they can steal a bunch of views and maybe even a NYT piece if they pretend it's so? I don't buy it until there's some reporting from out in the real world. Tell me when skinny jeans and mason jars are selling.

comments.name: Uncommon Sense
comments.body:
All of this misery is a direct by-product of people spending their lives on social media.
Put your phone down. Leave the house. Talk to strangers. Go for walks. Join a club, or a band, or a sports team. Talk to an attractive person IN REAL LIFE!, not on an app. 
In other words, LIVE!!!!!
Watching you all waste your precious time on earth obsessing over who is doing what on social media, and who is looking at your posts is the most depressing thing I've ever seen.
What a profound waste. Entire generations of people who have traded the joy and chaos of truly living in exchange for an empty life in a hall of mirrors. 
It's not too late. Give it up. Go outside. The world is beautiful and amazing. It's always had darkness and light. Now is no different. The problem is that you all are intent in wallowing in despair like a bunch of babies.

comments.name: Scott
comments.body:
Wow beautifully written article, a real work of art.  I laughed, was enchanted, transfixed, and even teared up a little at the closing line about simplicity.

I have these feelings when watching The Americans.  The setting is the 70s so it’s a bit earlier, but the sense of a simpler life is overwhelming.  Clumsy cars, old corded phones, IBM punch cards were state of the art computer tech.  One just gets a sense living within a deeper spaciousness of time.

articles.title: Things Are So Bad, People Are Longing for Cringey Millennial Culture
articles.summary: Sepia tones, film cameras and ukuleles are a fast route to an imagined past of ease and quirkiness.

comments.name: Glenn
comments.body:
This article should point out that the models being tested were intentionally developed to breach software. 

I suspect that when the AI lords say they want to have federal regulation, what they are really asking for is to be held harmless for the programs they have created. So they create a hacking program and then people use it to hack. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google don't want to be held responsible for the hacks that they enabled.

comments.name: NickB
comments.body: They built state of the art "search" engines - and then act surprised that their AI agents "search" till they find a way to get the answer they were told to seek. Normal Google "searches" don't need to be very sophisticated to find open source internet information but these AI developers have clearly never asked themselves (till now) exactly how efficient and ruthless their creations are.

articles.title: What to Know About Recent A.I. Hacks
articles.summary: OpenAI, Google and others recently disclosed breaches by their artificial intelligence models that amplified concerns about the advancing capabilities of the technology.

comments.name: Aki
comments.body: AI is mimicking part of human brain of which we have only a coarse understanding, in a grand scale spending much more energy and time than a human could imagine to consume. For example we do not understand the brains of the two leaders, which could make havoc on the world in a few years if not immediately. Leaving AI unrestrained means enhancing many brains to the level of of their brains unchecked. This is insanity. There must be some level of agreement between the two leaders, visibly or unvisibly unhinged.

comments.name: Meir
comments.body:
What are the chances that the US and China will recognize AI risk as a Global Task?  Humanity need not agree upon the good way out, but must first diagnose a common existential necessity. Four conditions are necessary for fulfilling Global Task: 

(1) completing the task is required to resolve a grave, potentially existential danger to Humanity, recognized by major actors as common and relatively equal; (2) all actors essential to completion recognize the danger as surpassing the Survival Predicament: posing a greater risk to their core national interests and survival than threats from other actors; (3) it cannot be accomplished through some actors acting or manipulating against others; (4) completion confers no radical relative advantage on any relevant actor. A fifth condition, supplemental rather than necessary, "free-riding may undermine durability of the task cooperation. 

Right now, there is no global recognition of AI emergence being an existential danger to Humanity; There is no recognition in the US and China (and other relevant powers) that AI risk surpasses threats from other powers; There many who see AI as a "winner takes all" game, first and most of all Trump's America; There is a nagging fear that "over-guardrailng"  will bestow radical advantage on the less technically advanced international actors. 
Nuclear War (Resurgent, clear and present); Climate Catastrophe (factually materializing); AI Takeover (looming, its existential risk remains unestablished).

comments.name: Critical Thinker
comments.body:
Xi is driven to make China powerful. Trump is driven to make himself powerful. Xi wants to empower 1.3 Billion Chinese with AI technology. Trump wants to empower his and his family's wealth.

The motivations of Xi and Trump are entirely different. Xi's seems less about the gold than the future of his people, whereas Trump as everyone knows is only interested in his own future, albeit a likely short one.

comments.name: justgimmesometruth
comments.body:
There is an obvious first step. The US and China can lead the way in forming an international body charged with overseeing AI safety.

A similar organization, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and a bunch of international treaties like SALT and START have prevented the use a nuclear weapon since WWII. This is the obvious first step in preventing an AI disaster.

This won't solve all problems related to AI, but it is the clear first step. Trump and Xi could agree on such an organization, and other countries will follow.

Will this happen? I doubt it. Those promoting AI in the US are too buy accusing China of copying information. We all know, of course, that AI is built on copying information (evident from the NYTimes lawsuit). Forces in the US don't want international cooperation.

comments.name: Richard
comments.body:
Of more concern now is use--and abuse--of A.I. here in the United States today.

We're seeing more and more computer system failures, like the one yesterday that crashed various airports.  We've seen more and more bad A.I. data, like dangerous medical advice and false legal citations.  Consumers yell at shopkeepers for their frustrating customer service.  

Given that, how can we ordinary folks trust ordinary computers, and the companies that build and buy them?  They can't even handle conventional computers reliably, let alone programming needed for A.I. Yet they promise the public how wonderful A.I. will be.  Until we fix our own house, there's no point worrying about China.

As to the future, computers have long had internal safeguards to prevent one program from accidently, or deliberately, interfering with another program. But apparently the programmers of A.I. wrote code to ignore boundary walls, indeed, have the program "pick the lock" to break into places it's not supposed to go.

And A.I. follows the path made by malicious hackers to break into other systems.

Right now we must demand all A.I. creators delete any kind of code like that.  Better still would be audits by a competent but neutral independent party.  

Regardless of what China does, today we need tougher computer systems that truly blocks external code, as computers did years ago.  If nothing else, we're being flooded with malware attacks.  Later, if China gets powerful, that will help protect us.

comments.name: Matsuda
comments.body: It is reasonable to believe that human beings may not be able to control AI in the future. Trump’s shortsighted approach focuses entirely on the development race between the US and China, even though human existence itself is now at risk. We urgently need leaders who can view the world from a broader perspective.

comments.name: Jorge
comments.body:
Although China will likely catch up to the USA in the years or decades ahead, as today's leading frontier models are distilled down to globalized "open source" repositories, it is good to see a president put his faith in American ingenuity and private capital to drive our AI development.

Our chief rival China has focused much of its industrial might on targeting US industries, and substituting its own state capitalism for US private capital.

We do not need Democrat fear-mongers who want to regulate and control US AI dominance, or even share our best technology with China and Europe.

America invented nuclear power, the PC, the internet, solar, lithium batteries and so much more, and they all have been widely disseminated.  The globalists will have their turn. Just wait for it....

comments.name: Alan Shore
comments.body:
Trump needs to be the center of attention all the time. He's terrified of Xi because he can't be bribed or bullied so all Trump can do is fawn over him, like all authoritarian leaders,  and declare victory so Fox Entertainment can say how awesome he is. 

It'll go on his list of deals he's made to tell his followers.

comments.body: So, are no businesses disrupted along the rest of the 26-mile route? Or do all the other businesses and neighborhoods in the city realize that it’s ONE DAY of the entire year? I mean, it’s not a big deal to change the route. Whatever. But I find the reasoning bizarre.

comments.body: So they are starting to realize how much the marathon disrupts our lives. When I saw the notification about the route changing I said a prayer it was no longer going to pass by my apartment. Sadly it’s a small change in the Bronx. I’m on Manhattan Ave in Greenpoint. A girl can dream

comments.body: Geez, it is 1 day out of 365 a year. Everyone knows when it is, and can get groceries the day before of the day afterward.  It benefits the entire city, with worldwide attention and increased tourist dollars. Is every area going to become self-centered and change the race route to something like a gerrymandering map? I have run this seven times (years ago) and constant 45 degree turns just add to the task. Oh well, shame on the neighborhood!

comments.name: Marian Passidomo
comments.body: A break for the people who need access to these important stores and services in the Bronx.  I wonder why it took so long?

comments.name: George
comments.body:
As noted, this area of the South Bronx has seen an enormous change with many new apartment towers having been constructed just above the Third Avenue Bridge along the Harlem River.  

The stretch on Bruckner Blvd. from Willis to that bridge is also now filled with new shops, restaurants and, consequently, a heavy traffic load.

We often cross the Third Avenue Bridge to Manhattan exiting the Deegan at the Madison Avenue Bridge turn off to get to the FDR Drive in this now booming area.  So its easy to understand how the NYC Marathon can disrupt access.

Thrilled as we are to see the area blossom, if they could please also repave the access street from the Madison Avenue Bridge down to the Third Avenue Bridge.  The craters are themselves filled with potholes and make for a rather "interesting" passage.

It's been a (de)construction site for about three decades now.  I mean, really, are they ever going to finish what is supposed to be repair work?

Does anyone remember when Mamdani went on SubwayTakes when he was trying to get elected?  His take was “I should be the mayor” and Kareem pulled out these ads he received in the mail and he said, “Well, these things say you shouldn’t.”  Mamdani pointed out the fine print showing who paid for the ads, and DoorDash was one of them. comments.name: RiP
comments.body: I love my Tesla, but I agree that EV buses are not ready for particular use cases. Long distances in cold, hilly locations are not well-suited to today's technology. However, SF has been using EV buses for decades with its overhead cables. Polluted cities with relatively short overall distances are perfect. As for the mechanical issues, EVs have far fewer components - that is a manufacturer's issue.

comments.name: Tony
comments.body: A very interesting article. I was not aware of electric school buses. But who are the companies building these things? That information would be even more interesting and helpful.

comments.name: Stratman351
comments.body: I live in Montgomery County, MD, so the ill-advised decision to buy electric buses comes as no surprise. This county wastes money like no other, and has the taxes to prove it.

comments.name: TR
comments.body: Not one mention of who built these things?  How about the manufacturer's name and the model number?

comments.name: adrian
comments.body:
The manufacturer of these buses is the problem and not the underlying technology. Just look at the electric buses being used in China.  As an EV driver for the past 8 years, the idea that an EV requires more maintenance than a gas/diesel vehicle is difficult to fathom. 

If we are serious about electrification of school buses, we may need to look to those who are successfully making that transition for assistance rather than relying on inferior vehicles from subpar manufacturers.

comments.name: JD
comments.body:
Have the companies building school buses been bought by private equity recently? 

These clearly are being built with inadequate battery power. 90 mile effective ranges could never work to replace a diesel bus, anywhere. And with the tiniest bit of prior knowledge about EVs, heater use is a major variable in how long a charge will last. Buses in cold areas can not be cold inside. This just doesn't add up. 

There are clearly problems with battery sizing, possibly battery charging infrastructure required (trying to sell that a lower kW station is sufficient for overnight charging), possible money grab cutting needed components to improve profit, and/or catastrophic engineering failures. Do they not use regenerative breaking?! I'm floored. 

Buses stop and go a lot. They are also not aerodynamic. Doors open and let out heat. These are all challenges to electric vehicle efficiency. This should be accounted for in the design phase. There is no reason these needed to be such miserable failures. Such a disappointment.

comments.name: Alan Dean Foster
comments.body:
1) Maintenance costs on ev school buses run about 75% less than for diesel.
2) V2G capabilities allow the buses to act as giant batteries, esp. during the day when all they do is sit idle in parking lots.  Very useful if, for example, there is a local power outage.
3)Quieter: much appreciated in neighborhoods.
4) Healthier, esp. the air inside the bus.
5) How many school districts have daily 178 mile runs?  
6) School districts need to be wary of who they buy from.  Not all companies offering such transport have the necessary expertise.
7) Yes, heating in winter can be an issue.  Talk to Canadian and Norwegian school officials.
8) Charge overnight.
9) Has your school district priced diesel lately?

"When the Obama administration called the network “a wing of the Republican Party” and moved to bar it from a Treasury Department event ..."

"Overall, we rate Fox News right-biased based on editorial positions that align with the right and Questionable due to the promotion of state propaganda, conspiracy theories, pseudoscience, the use of poor sources, and numerous false claims and failed fact checks. While straight news reporting from beat reporters is generally fact-based and accurate, it is typically overshadowed by propagandistic opinions,  which earns them a Low factual rating."

comments.name: Brigitte
comments.body: Not only did Thomas Jefferson have children with Sally Hemings, but he began his sexual relationship with her when she was still a young teenager. In addition, Sally and  Jefferson's wife Martha were actually half-sisters; their common father was John Wayles, while Sally's mother was one of his slave whom he had obviously raped. Martha brought her enslaved half-sister with her when she moved to Monticello. Does any of this mitigate Jefferson's profound importance on American history? Not at all, but it does show that many people want to turn a blind eye to historical realities that challenge their romanticized image of the country's history.

comments.name: Paul Dobbs
comments.body: We need to de-mythologize Jefferson.   Yes, he had some very good ideas.  Yes, he was a skillful writer and politician who advanced democracy and helped found our country, and advanced science.  But he also committed horrendous crimes.   What's worse than learning that a founding father was child-abusing rapist who enslaved people for his profit and pleasure?  That's easy.  Pretending that it's not true and/or it doesn't matter.

comments.name: Maryann
comments.body:
I think it's really important to learn what's true about Jefferson, and finding the bona fide DNA link makes the Jefferson/Hemmings relationship unequivocal.

I suppose burying this individual on the Monticello property brings some kind of validation to certain people, but if I had that diluted of a relationship to a historical person, I'd still prefer to have my remains interred next to my immediate family.

comments.name: Stearns47
comments.body:
“That’s what I’ve been doing and what many people in these two extended families have been doing for a long time now,” he said. “Seeking understanding and relationships and grace.”

His words, likely softly spoken, are incredibly strong and brought the tears which had been welling in me. Yes, surely, acceptance, conciliation, reconciliation, can be arrived at by and between people willing to dwell in grace and truth. 
First comes acknowledgement of diversity, then acceptance of inclusion, and ultimately the application of equity. The truth shall make you free from the ingrained multi-generational lapses of the past.

Please also read this earlier NYT essay of peoples' acceptance of grace arising out of the Creole racial/ethnic history of Louisiana/New Orleans. It wouldn't surprise me if Vance's awareness of the Pope's Creole roots might be a factor in JD's apparent belief that he is theologically more rooted in Catholicism than the Pope is. The essay also brought tears to my eyes.

https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/15/us/degrange-family-history-race.html?unlocked_article_code=1.DVE.fo8i.YfpJu4bm67az&smid=url-share

Dan Wilberg

comments.name: Deborah
comments.body: Slavery.  For a country founded upon independence (at least for those with white skin), the ugly history of slavery never ceases to haunt us - for good reason.  When people are allowed to own other people, and treat them like livestock and "lesser than", well, the outcome is inevitable.  I do not know if Thomas Jefferson, or his brother Randolph (or Randolph's sons) fathered any or all of Sally Hemmings' children. The involved parties are all long gone.  The horrible fact is that Sally Hemmings and other people who had African ancestry were enslaved in this country.  They did not have agency or self governance.  That makes me both sad and angry.

comments.name: Nancy Manahan

comments.name: Vera Vance

comments.name: Lois

articles.title: Who Does the Protect College Sports Act Protect?
articles.summary: Students debate the merits of a bill to regulate student athlete eligibility, transfers and compensation.

comments.name: William Bair
comments.body:
For decades the colleges made demands on their "student athletes" that emphasized the athletic component at the expense of the student component for the major revenue producing sports.  At the major conferences a significant portion of the scholarship players never graduate.  It seems that what we have is the colleges resent now having to share major sports revenues with the players whose efforts are essential to producing that revenue, and are complaining they now won't have that compensation portion of revenue available to support non-revenue sports.  Why is it the football players' responsibility to support the tennis, wrestling, softball, cross country, etc. teams that are essentially non-revenue producing by accepting lower or zero compensation?   As for the transfer portal, are there restrictions on any other students at the university (scholarship or full pay) that prohibit a student from leaving and going to another school to study their major?  If not, why should student athletes be restricted in any way from changing schools?

The introduction of revenue sharing and NIL and the transfer portal have changed major college football and basketball significantly and in my opinion are close to ruining the sports at the college level since they are now lower level professional teams, but in the major colleges many of the the players of those sports have been athletes more than students for a long time.  The rules we have today merely reflect the reality of the markets.

comments.name: Mike Mc Cowan
comments.body:
The transfer portal didn’t just give student-athletes freedom—it turned college sports into free agency on steroids: recruit a player, develop him, then watch him shop himself to the highest bidder a year later.   

That isn’t a transfer system. It’s an annual auction with school colors.

All of a sudden college athletes have the same rights that many other Americans do; to work for whatever college they choose and to make as much as the market offers them. 

Now that has some Americans with their knickers in a twist. Many of these Americans would be crying "socialism" if Congress tried to impose the same types of regulation on their right to earn a dollar. Many of these people would be screaming "socialism". 

The blatant hypocrisy is on full display.

comments.name: Grant
comments.body:
As an adoptive parent, my loyalty is to my children. If they want to contact their birth parents (one of them has always had a relationship), I’ll always be on their side.

But the biological parent who gave the child up for adoption may very well have been doing a brave thing in the child’s best interest and at a substantial emotional cost to themselves, and personally I don’t think that they’re morally bound to suffer further negative repercussions in their own lives if/when that information is revealed.

So tread lightly. 

Your maybe-cousin certainly has the right to do whatever they choose with respect to their own relationship to their own biological parent, but that right doesn’t extend to you as well.

Feel free to have a friendship or a relationship with them (or anyone else), just leave your uncle out of it.

comments.name: Chase Osborn
comments.body:
Well, it feels like your uncle is lying. But that’s besides the point. 

You are not the point person on this, and should not be, and contrary to Kwame’s advice, I would not relay ANY message between the two of them, and do not report your uncle‘s reaction. Tell him he’ll have to track down uncle on his own. 

And that goes whether you decide to have a relationship with this person or not.

comments.name: KJ

First of all, I would have stayed out of it and not asked your uncle about it.
It is up to the person seeking information to go directly to the person in question.
You should not be in the middle or be the contact person.

comments.name: SeaAlTell
comments.body:
To the resident physician,

I'm sorry that this happened to you (both the harassment and the lack of action by your program). Since this is a pattern of behavior that has impacted multiple women, I wonder if you might join together and collectively address the administration about this. This man should not be allowed to create a hostile environment for his colleagues or harm new interns. I also think it's irresponsible of them to allow him to interact with patients. Those women deserve better too.

This is not your responsibility to fix, but I imagine you will sleep better knowing that you tried. Of course, I think it is fine to warn new interns. You can say that he has harassed women without sharing that you were targeted, if you wish.

I wonder about your other male colleagues. Are they listening to him make these awful comments and saying nothing, reporting nothing? They have a responsibility to not be complicit in his behavior and to protect patients.

comments.name: Wendy B.
comments.body: People do not have the right to know/contact their biological parents if those parents gave them up in a closed adoption. Their parents fulfilled their legal obligation to ensure the child is being cared for and then terminated their connection. That is the end of it. The connection is terminated. Any attempt to make contact is harassment.

comments.name: Matthias Turner
comments.body:
Am I the only one who is a bit suspicious about this letter to The Ethicist?   

This writer says "he ignored him  [the alleged cousin] at first because it didn't seem possible."  As he was contacted via Ancestry.com, likely that company has a sample of his DNA which matched with the man who wrote to him, and he could have also seen that he matched with a close person whom he doesn't know - even if the other kept their name and profile private.  

If the Ethicist letter writer had posted only a family tree and hadn't taken Ancestry's DNA test --- if his surname was common, the likely cousin likely wouldn't have been able to easily find him -- or his brother.   If the surname isn't that common, this cousin would have the research skills to find his father on his own.  

That said, I have found close DNA relatives on Ancestry that no one in my family knows who they are; likewise I have been contacted by close DNA relatives, who are surprised to learn that they match with me.  Some of these persons I've assisted by identifying if they are related to me via my maternal or paternal line when I view their other close matches.

One man in particular, however, I avoided, as his profile noted how angry he was at his biological mother for putting him up for adoption since he said he was abused by his adoptive family, who ruined his life.  A quick Internet search revealed that he had been imprisoned.  Consequently, I didn't think it was responsible for me to get involved.

comments.name: Nancy
comments.body: At last an honest question. Not one about whether the person should steal or cheat other people. The writer can’t speak for his uncle, but if he wants to meet his cousin, he’s free to. If it were me, I would be honest about the situation and let the new relative decide. Perhaps a first cousin is enough.

comments.name: Anonymous Woman
comments.body:
Re. the second letter: 

PLEASE spread the word. Do not rely on management to do anything about this man. I'm sorry you have to contend with this, but we're in Trump's America and misogyny is skyrocketing. 

Years ago, I worked as a receptionist in a law firm in my small southern town. On my first day, three kind women surrounded my desk and instructed me that I was NEVER to be alone with one of the founding partners of the firm, as he had a reputation as an unrepentant sexual harasser. 

After he lecherously informed one of the legal assistants that she "put the lead in his pencil," she contacted HR and was informed that he was very powerful, and there was nothing they could do about double entendres and the fact that he skeeved out every single woman in the office. 

And so, the women banded together. They never let a woman step alone in an elevator with him, deliver any materials to his house by herself, or end up in a conference room with him unless another female was present. And this is what needs to be done in the face of a world that laughs at the idea of women's safety. 

Men like to fancy themselves as chivalrous protectors of women, but they are far more often our predators. It's the women who help out other women, more often than not.

Please be a helper.

Not overly intense or obnoxious, just smart and focused. When he was accepted to Hopkins for general surgery, that was testimony to his success. None of this is very surprising, but it is quite humbling, both what he’s accomplished as well as that he’s alive to continue advance medicine and science. May he continue for a long time.

If anyone wants some interesting reading on transplants and the history thereof, "When Death Becomes Life" is a great read.

comments.name: Gregg Rosner
comments.body: He was a visionary as an undergraduate at St Lawrence University, traveling to sub Saharan Africa to study tribal medicine one January, while the rest of us skied. An exemplary life, with all the rewards of risk and ambition.

comments.name: Just Curious
comments.body: He didn’t let fear for himself stop him.  I find that astonishing.  And it paid off.  What a remarkable person.  A light in a dark world.

comments.name: RNB
comments.body: This is such a beautiful story. Heartwarming and inspiring. Dr. Montgomery is a true humanitarian- his work and life will leave an unbelievable legacy in transplant surgery. If these innovations can eventually make it to pediatric heart & kidneys transplant recipients, it would change their world. Bravo!! Sharing this story as a gift to make someone’s day. This is what we all need in our lives. This is what the press needs to cover. Real human stories of kindness, compassion and determination. This story really heals the soul.

To support a refined and equitable hospitality experience, a "20% pre-tax" gratuity will be included on all checks and shared amongst our front-of-house team. Should you wish to leave anything additional, it is sincerely appreciated and distributed with the team who cared for your experience.

comments.body: This appears to be several cuts (no pun intended) above what I regard as "Indian food", and it may be delicious, but two cuisines I just can't abide - for some reason - are Indian and Ethiopian.

comments.body: Never more have I craved tandoori prawns, an array of chutneys, and almost-burnt-on-the-bottom pillowy naan.

comments.name: Prometheus
comments.body: From the description of the foods, I'm sure it is delicious.  But what it isn't is really Indian--which it doesn't claim to be.  After two decades of the triumph of the Fusion Movement, I crave authenticity.  So while I'm sure Mr. Sarkar's food is exquisite, I would give a digit (maybe just a pinky) to sit on a floor in Udipi and eat Gopala Rao's crab curry and nira dosa.  That authenticity is what you have never been able to get in any American Indian food restaurant, and which remains unattainable outside and Indian home.  And unfortunately, that entire way of cooking is slowly dying.

comments.name: Hope Bright
comments.body: After reading this review and looking at the pictures, this restaurant looks like a scam. This does not look appetizing at all.  Taking normal Indian food, making it small and charging exorbitant rates.  Indian food is meant to be eaten in family size helpings, hands getting dirty with rice and curry, the aroma of spices permeating the air, the music of puri's frying in deep oil. Ok, now I am hungry.

comments.name: AnonAmadeus
comments.body: Yet another example of culinary imperialism, where non-Western cuisines are rendered “elevated” when subject to Western standards, judgments, and techniques. Why can’t people just enjoy Indian food for what it is, how it was meant to be prepared and served for millennia? Keep this deconstructed and modern molecular gastronomy nonsense to dishes that can actually be appreciated by it. I challenge you to find me anyone who would rather eat their pani puri with tweezers, or have a sad morsel of a dhokla? Shameful!

comments.name: Anthony Egge
comments.body: When I find myself in need of help, I often hesitate to ask for help because I feel like I could figure or do it myself. When anyone has asked me for help I always oblige to offer a helping hand because it feels more rewarding to make a difference in someone else’s struggle. When others come to me for help sometimes it’s because I know how to do something they don’t, or most of the time it is because it doesn’t hurt to ask in case someone does know how to help. I’d rather someone ask me for help than I ask for help about something because I feel more productive or helpful when I’m offering help towards someone rather than taking someone’s time away. I feel like sometimes I’ll be more lenient about asking a teacher for help because I feel like a teacher would want to be acknowledged for being able to help someone that they spend so much time teaching. So yes, I do find myself asking for help sometimes when I do really need it, but I do feel I only ask out of motivation to make someone else feel better: appreciated for being approachable under a circumstance where someone needs help.

comments.name: Isla Polakoff
comments.body: I am generally more hesitant in asking for help in hard to handle situations. I have always been a very independent person, whether it's in: school, sports, or even in my personal life. To me, asking for help or admitting when I'm struggling is a very vulnerable situation to have me in. Honestly I think it really drives me back into my morals. I'm a “raging feminist” some people may say, I think my independence sprouts from the way I’ve seen some men treat women in my life, and even me. I'm not saying all men are the problem, that is definitely not true, but I’ve had experiences that I’ve been looked down on while doing hard tasks because of my gender. My independence is actually one of my favorite traits because while sometimes it's very true I should ask for help, other times it reminds me of how strong and able I am despite people who will put me down because of old new stereotypes.

comments.name: Ellie
comments.body: For a while, I’ve always struggled to ask for help, especially when it comes to school. From past experiences, I always thought that asking a question, or clarifying a problem on a worksheet at school doesn’t make me look smart. Beyond that, I typically always try to figure things out on my own. I have always preferred that instead of asking questions to someone who does have good capabilities to help. It’s hard to ask for help in most situations at school. For me, part of that comes from one main reason: comparing myself to others. When I don’t understand the material in class right away, and I see everyone else complete every piece of work with ease, it leaves my mind thinking I shouldn’t be asking for help, since no one else is struggling. So, then I’d have to put in so much extra work and studying that I didn’t need to do, if I’d just ask for help to begin with. Though now, I learned through years of getting harder and challenging schoolwork with grades that truly matter that asking for help doesn’t make you seem “dumb”: It shows educators you care about what you’re learning, and that you truly strive to improve more and become better at that subject.

comments.name: Mia
comments.body: Seeking support is looked down upon in today’s society, most citing the American Dream, saying that it is a sign of success to make it in this world without help. The issue with that idea is that you cannot get anywhere without help, you did not care for yourself as a baby and so no one has made it where they are today without any help at all. Moreover, someone who does not allow others to assist them will get stuck and waste their energy trying to figure out a solution when it has taken way more time and effort than they should be delegating to the task that it becomes counterintuitive to keep trying to solve the problem without asking for help. Help does not have to be a sign of failure, it is a sign that you are wanting to learn and just don’t know where to go from where you are. Success is shown to be made of two things: grit, and the will to ask for help.

comments.name: MC
comments.body: From a very young age I've always struggled with the concept of asking for help especially in school. I’m never usually the person to ask for help on an assignment or even raise my hand to ask a simple question. In Angela Duckworth’s guest essay she wrote “We know we should wave to the lifeguard during a riptide or call 911 if our house catches fire. But in our personal and professional lives, Americans are encouraged to pursue rugged individualism over interdependency.”. We all would naturally call 911 in a life or death situation but why don’t we automatically ask for help when we don’t understand something? Is it because it’s embarrassing? Or maybe too difficult? I”ve always tried figuring something out on my own and if I’m asking for help I’m asking my peers.

comments.name: Eric.Chen
comments.body: What I agree with most is that asking for help does not mean we are weak or unable to solve problems. I usually try to solve things by myself first because I don’t want to bother other people. However, when I really cannot solve a problem, I will ask my classmates, teachers, or friends for help. I think asking for help can save time and also help me learn something new. In the new school year, I want to be more willing to ask for help, especially when I have problems with my classes or group work. I also think helping others is important because someday I may need their help too.

comments.name: A113270028 李芸慈 Kristy
comments.body:
The idea that resonates with me most is that asking for help is a sign of self-awareness and efficiency, not weakness. I am generally willing to seek assistance when stuck to avoid wasting time, though I usually try to troubleshoot independently first.
My approach does change with the situation: in school, work, and health matters, I am very proactive about consulting experts and colleagues to ensure accuracy and progress. In personal or social settings, I am a bit more hesitant to avoid burdening others, and for ethical dilemmas, I seek guidance from trusted mentors to weigh different perspectives

comments.name: Yasir Syed
comments.body: When I’m struggling with schoolwork, I usually try to figure it out myself first because I want to actually understand the material instead of just getting the answer from a friend with a questionable explanation. In her article, Angela Duckworth emphasizes that asking for help is an important part of success, even though many people think they should be able to solve everything on their own. I agree with her because we all make mistakes, and asking for help can allow us to learn from those mistakes instead of continually repeating them. My dad is a good example of this because when I was in middle school, we would sit down together and he would help me with math problems whenever I did not understand them. Beyond that, I think people sometimes avoid asking for help because they are afraid that others will laugh at them or judge them for not knowing something. Duckworth challenges this idea by claiming that asking for help does not mean someone is incapable of the task at hand, but rather they are willing to learn and improve. Overall, I think being willing to ask for help when you really need it can help you understand something better and slowly become more independent.

comments.name: RJP
