An essay on relations between China and the US that urges both sides to act responsibly and rationally and does not mention Taiwan. Really? 
 
China seeks to take Taiwan by force or through coercion in the next decade (my guess is 2028 when Trump is still president and certainly will not respond militarily), expand and deepen its regional hegemony, and 60 years from now to have the 21st century be called "the Chinese century." 

In short, China is early 20th century Germany with historical grievances and grand aspirations but with an exponentially bigger country and a totalitarian regime. It is not willingly going to act responsibly or rationally.  
 
Our great advantages in restraining China were its neighbors' fear of China and respect for America's word, rough sense of fairness, and power. Yes, encirclement. But today how can any foreign nation have any faith in what we say and what we might do? By casting doubt on our credibility and our values, and by increasingly signaling that we will not use military forces to challenge Chinese aggression in Asia, we are emboldening China. It is going to be a wild ride.

This quote illustrates the stark underestimation of who has greater leverage : "Beijing, for its part, must recognize that every time it weaponizes its dominance of critical minerals, it hastens U.S. efforts to diversify its own supply chains, thereby eroding China’s leverage and hardening American fears about Beijing’s intentions." It would take years for the US to be able to match the rare earth production capabilities of China, who controls 91% of the world's rare earth metals. If China weaponizes their control it would damage everyone's economy but the US would be the biggest loser. National security experts note that periodic truces actually weaken the urgency for Western companies to build independent supply chains, leaving the U.S. vulnerable. Don't you think China could figure out chip design faster than we could come up with rare earth metals?

But I heard a credible source discuss that idea of banning export of US-produced diesel would put refiners in a bind since that would result in having to figure out what to do with the extra diesel produced after you've stored lots. We don't consume 20% of production and after you can't store the extra you lose one fraction of an input barrel that you suddenly can't sell. Profits go down and eventually output of other products fractioned from the same barrel go down.

"There is no switch that can make diesel prices go down in a week" is the quote at the end of this article.

But here's what diesel prices did do each week this month, according to the EIA in their weekly published update on US gasoline and diesel:

Sep 7 - $5.967/gallon

Sep 21 - $6.529/gallon (up another 24 cents)

comments.name: A geologist

NYTimes coverage of individual weather phenomenon like Polo and roaming heat domes, as well as broad comprehensive consequences of warming air and oceans leading to cascading impacts driven by climate change, is exceptional.

Mr. Harlan detailed the social/political debate of which "existential" threat is more immediate and critical, A.I. or climate change? Both are really bad.

The science of climate change is documented & known, modeling impacts are extremely complicated is the lesson Mr. Wallace-Wells details. Regardless of modeled predictions, the reality has turned out to be worse, involving more complex feedbacks than predicted. There are no good outcomes, impacts will only get much worse, outstripping infrastructure and the favorable environmental conditions that sustain life. Rising temps accelerated 2x in last 25 yrs.

Exxon scientists 1980s back-of-envelope modeling accurately predicted future temps and threats. The physics of climate change is undeniable.

Paralysis is what happens when critical things are not addressed. Our brains are not wired to effectively manage everything hitting us at once, people can't synthesize existential threats--that's what scientists do.

comments.name: T.K. Small

I have received CDPAP services for more than 30 years and have worked in healthcare policy for many years. From both a personal and professional standpoint, the transition to PPL and the unionization of these workers are steps in the wrong direction.

The changes to CDPAP under Gov. Hochul were instigated by 1199 for the purpose of making it easier to organize these workers. Certainly, the overall CDPAP budget line had grown to an estimated $11 billion, but that was due to mismanagement and corruption in Albany. How can the benefits of a no-bid contract to an out-of-state company with a shady track record be taken seriously?

The idea that there are 70,000 signatures from people who want to join the union is really more a statement about the dissatisfaction with PPL. Regularly, PPL makes payroll mistakes, and CDPAP workers are underpaid or not paid at all! Finally, I doubt the state is saving money with PPL. While the administrative budget line of CDPAP has gone down, the hourly rate that PPL bills Medicaid has gone up.

It produced the decades-long delay between drug development and general availability.  It caused the billion-dollar price tag for developing new drugs. Today, we are witnessing the sorry spectacle of the United Nations reduced to a mere power-sharing arrangement among the most dominant nations, leaving absolutely no room for middle powers or the Global South. This systemic exclusion is the exact reason Iran—and others on the outside looking in—behave the way they do out of sheer desperation and defiance.

Yet, while the digital and AI revolution has fundamentally democratized influence and empowered the traditionally "meek" to disrupt old power structures, the United States continues to operate as if nothing has changed. Clinging to outdated dominance while ignoring the realities of a multipolar, technologically fractured world will inevitably cost Washington—and global stability—very dearly.

comments.name: Jon W
comments.body:
“Faster, cheaper and safer” sounds like an extraordinary combination. But I’m not sure the article gives us enough information to know what “safer” actually means.

If some sensitive requests are now identified and routed away from the frontier model to an older, more restricted model, how much of the reported safety improvement reflects better judgment by the new model, and how much reflects a reduction in the possibilities available to the overall system?

There’s an old word for deliberately restricting a horse’s freedom of movement so it can’t wander off and hurt itself or cause damage: hobbling. A hobbled horse may indeed be safer. But that doesn’t mean the horse itself has learned to behave more safely.

The same question applies to performance. If capabilities or paths through a problem have been restricted, are speed comparisons being made across equivalent possibility spaces?

None of this means Anthropic’s approach is wrong. Restricting capabilities may be excellent safety engineering. But “the model became intrinsically safer” and “we made the system safer by limiting what the model can do” are different accomplishments.

Anthropic reports an 85% reduction in bad outcomes in one containment evaluation. Impressive—but I’d like to know how much came from a better-trained horse, and how much came from the hobble.

If an eight-year old can figure this out, why can't Trump? Oh, I forgot: My grandson isn't beholden to t=oil companies. 

Under the Biden administration's rebate progra, we installed a geothermal heating/AC system. One of the things that could be done to help climate change would be to require all new construction to install geothermal, since there's already a big hole in the ground for all new construction. The system works great. It's expensive if the house already exists and the hole in the ground has to be dug, but it's an amazing way to heat and cool one's home. comments.name: Federalist
comments.body:
My issue with the outgoing Secretary General is not his warning us of the dire future we face it is that he is over-optimistic. Likewise Mr. Gelles. 

It is clear from the ongoing rise in CO2 in the atmosphere and the ongoing rise in methane and other greenhouse gases that we are making zero progress in protecting the Earth from transition to a new Hot House Earth equilibrium. Progress in installation of alternative energy is more than undone by continued expansion of fossil fuel use and production. Research by scientists such as Johan Rockstrom finds that we are already passing tipping points, passing interacting Planetary Boundaries that are like dominoes, in that passing one pushes over another in a self accelerating cascade.  This while fossil fuel production still increases. 

The transition to Hot House Earth is close to becoming self accelerating.  Yet we ignore the scientific evidence, such as the observed slowing of the AMOC  and accelerating ice cap melt, showing that this is happening. Losing control, triggering the Earth System to transition, means losing the stable environment that fostered the expansion of modern humans and the origin of our civilization. 

It means entering a population bottleneck during the unstable transition centuries that reduce food production below carrying capacity. It means famines, great floods that destroy infrastructure and droughts that reduce food production. 

Over-optimistic reporting is part of the problem.

I remember one little hole-in-the wall store on 4th Avenue which had been a luncheonette, with a painted-over Coke sign on the facade, where I found tons of mint issues of "Galaxy" and the British "New Worlds," the latter  inexplicably stamped with the name "Gordon & Gotch," an Australian magazine and book importer. How they got from the UK to Australia and thence to the USA will forever remain a mystery.

comments.name: Jr. AmericanPoliticalDevelopmentScholar
comments.body:
Fehrenbacher, Don E. The Dred Scott Case: Its Significance in American Law and Politics. Oxford, England: Oxford University Press, 1978. 
This Pulitzer prize winner is less than two hundred but more than a hundred twenty five, let’s just say 151, of books I’ve read twice.
The first time as an academic document, second time as a Bible, the text each side used as a rallying cry.
“If thy right hand offend thee, cut it off” vs. “if your eye causes you to sin: pluck it out, [cuz it’s better to lose an eye than descend into hell] takes on a new dimension: the existence of the TexasCourt of CriminalAppeals.
TheSupremeCourt has held Texas never actually seceded from TheUnion—Texas v. White, 74 U.S. (7 Wall.) 700 (1869)—but never declared its segregated civil/criminal supreme courts unconstitutional as the Thirteenth Amendment enables.
Dred Scott v. Sandford, 60 U.S. (19 How.) 393 (1857), written by ChiefJustice Roger B. Taney—Andrew Jackson’s Secretary of the Treasury, appointed Attorney General after the Second Bank of the United States refused to withdraw the federal government’s payments—served as secessionist New Testament. Read a second time more slowly, I cannot help but to condemn CharlesEvansHughes, who resigned from the Supreme Court in 1916 to run against Woodrow Wilson, founder of the American Realm of Political Science (Johns Hopkins PhD: Congressional Government.) 
Hughes viewed Dred Scott as an aberration of the Taney judiciary. 
Now who’s the white supremacist?
